explanations.answer: On their hearts and their altars
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says the sin is engraved "…on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars." So it's carved into the inside of the people and into the place where they worshiped. A diamond point isn't something you wipe off with a damp rag.

explanations.answer: On their foreheads and their hands
explanations.explanation: Foreheads and hands is a fair guess, friend, but it's not what the LORD says. He says the sin is engraved "…on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars." The hearts and the altars carry it, and I think that's a heavy picture.

explanations.answer: On their doorposts and their gates
explanations.explanation: Doorposts and gates would at least be places you could scrub, friend. But the LORD says the sin is engraved "…on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars." It's written on the hearts and on the altars, not on the house.

Close, baker, but the LORD says the opposite. He says, "Even their children remember their altars and Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills." So the children haven't forgotten these things. They remember them.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Even their children remember their altars and Asherah poles by the green trees and on the high hills." So the claim that they've forgotten is false, because the text says they remember. The children aren't forgetting a thing, and I think that's what makes this verse so heavy.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, "…I will give over your wealth and all your treasures as plunder, because of the sin of your high places…" Plunder is what enemies carry off. The treasures aren't staying put.

Hiding treasure in the hills sounds like a smart move, friend, but that's not what the LORD says. He says, "…I will give over your wealth and all your treasures as plunder…" Nothing in these verses says the treasure gets tucked away safe. It gets handed over.

Storing treasure in the temple would feel safe, baker, but the LORD doesn't say that here. He says, "…I will give over your wealth and all your treasures as plunder, because of the sin of your high places…" The treasures go out as plunder, not into storage.

explanations.answer: In a land they do not know
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "I will enslave you to your enemies in a land that you do not know…" It's not just that they lose the inheritance. They end up somewhere unfamiliar. I think that's a hard thing to hear.

I get why you'd think that, friend, but the LORD says something different. He says, "I will enslave you to your enemies in a land that you do not know…" So it's not their own land. It's a land that is strange to them.

explanations.answer: Back in the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt is a famous place for slavery, baker (Exodus 1:13, 14), but this verse never says it. The LORD says, "I will enslave you to your enemies in a land that you do not know…" He doesn't name the land here. He says it's one they don't know.

Right on, baker. The LORD says the man who trusts in mankind "…will be like a shrub in the desert…" A shrub out in the desert. Hardly a picture of someone who's doing well.
A river is the opposite of what the LORD pictures, friend. He says this man "…will be like a shrub in the desert…" There's no river anywhere in that verse. It's all dry.

A cedar sounds mighty, baker, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says the man who trusts in mankind "…will be like a shrub in the desert…" A shrub, out in the desert. That's a big step down from mighty.
Yes, baker. The LORD says of this man, "he will not see when prosperity comes." Good things can come, and he still doesn't see them. That's a hard way to live.

That's right, baker. The man who trusts in the LORD is "…like a tree planted by the waters…" Compare that to the shrub in the desert. This tree is planted right where the water is.

Branches get all the attention, friend, but the LORD points down. This tree "…sends out its roots toward the stream." The roots are what reach for the water.
Seeds are a creative guess, baker, but they're not in the verse. The LORD says the tree "…sends out its roots toward the stream." It's the roots that head for the water.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind…" The question was who can understand the heart, and here's the answer. He can.
Priests are a reasonable guess, friend, but they're not mentioned here. The LORD says, "I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind…" He's the one doing the searching.

explanations.answer: A man who makes a fortune unjustly
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, "Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly." A partridge sitting on eggs she did not lay. That's the picture of a fortune made unjustly.

explanations.answer: A man who leaves his father's house
explanations.explanation: Leaving home is a common thing to guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, "Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly." It's about money made the wrong way.

explanations.answer: A man who works on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Good thinking on the Sabbath, baker, but it's not what this verse says. The LORD says, "Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly." The picture is about a fortune made unjustly.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "In the middle of his days his riches will desert him, and in the end he will be the fool." So the money doesn't last. The fortune walks out on him.
That's right, baker. The LORD says, "In the middle of his days his riches will desert him, and in the end he will be the fool." The riches don't stay all his days. They leave him partway through.

explanations.answer: Shame for them but not for him
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The prayer says, "Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame." It's the cry of someone being persecuted. I think it's a hard prayer, and the text just lets it stand.

explanations.answer: Shame for him but not for them
explanations.explanation: That's flipped around, friend. The prayer says, "Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame." The shame he asks for lands on the ones persecuting him, not on himself.

explanations.answer: No shame for anyone at all
explanations.explanation: That would be a gentle prayer, baker, but it's not this one. The prayer says, "Let my persecutors be put to shame, but do not let me be put to shame." So he asks for shame to land on them, and for it to stay off him.
